# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterised by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of significant epicardial coronary stenosis. CSFP is defined as angiographically evident delayed distal coronary opacification during selective coronary angiography, occurring in the absence of significant epicardial coronary artery stenosis (luminal diameter reduction less than 40%), and epidemiologic studies estimate its prevalence at 1–5% among patients undergoing coronary angiography. The condition was first reported more than five decades ago. It was first described by Tambe et al. in 1972. Because the underlying disturbance lies in the resistance microvessels rather than the conduit arteries, CSFP is now regarded as a discrete coronary microvascular disorder, sometimes termed "cardiac syndrome Y" [1,2]. The coronary slow flow phenomenon is an angiographic finding characterized by delayed distal vessel opacification in the absence of significant epicardial coronary disease.

Importantly, primary CSFP must be distinguished from secondary causes of slow flow. "Primary" CSFP should be distinguished from delayed contrast progression in the context of coronary reperfusion therapy such as angioplasty or stenting for acute myocardial infarction, or other "secondary" causes that include coronary artery ectasia, coronary artery spasm, valvular heart disease, or connective tissue disorders.

## Diagnosis

Diagnosis is angiographic and increasingly quantitative. Although the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) flow grade is a valuable and widely used qualitative measure in angiographic trials, it is limited by its subjective and categorical nature; the number of cineframes needed for dye to reach standardized distal landmarks can be counted to objectively assess coronary blood flow as a continuous variable. The corrected TIMI frame count (cTFC), introduced by Gibson and colleagues, standardises this measure for the longer left anterior descending artery. In normal arteries the LAD frame count (36.2 ± 2.6 frames) was 1.7 times longer than the mean of the right coronary and circumflex counts. In practice, diagnosis is made by demonstration of either TIMI-2 flow or a corrected TIMI frame count greater than 27 frames, in addition to no angiographic lesions of 40% or more and delayed distal vessel opacification in at least one epicardial vessel. CSFP is now also embedded within consensus definitions of microvascular dysfunction: the 2018 COVADIS consensus statement lists the coronary slow-flow phenomenon, defined by a corrected TIMI frame count greater than 25, among the criteria for diagnosing coronary microvascular dysfunction. However, the equivalence of cTFC with invasive indices is debated; recent invasive work suggests that angiographic slow flow correlates with microvascular resistance but is an imperfect surrogate for coronary flow reserve [3,4].

## Clinical presentation and prognosis

The typical patient is a young male smoker. The most common group with CSFP is young males with a history of smoking. A large prevalence study confirmed key associations: CSFP is associated with male sex and obesity, and multivessel involvement may be a marker of more severe, diffuse disease. Hypertension, dyslipidaemia and tobacco use also feature prominently as independent correlates [5,6].

Although once considered benign, CSFP carries real clinical consequences. The clinical implications are significant, with over 80% of patients experiencing recurrent chest pain, resulting in considerable impairment in quality of life. The presentation spans the acute coronary syndrome spectrum. CSFP has a diverse presentation from mild chest discomfort to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, and it can have severe morbidity and mortality implications. Arrhythmic risk is increasingly recognised; a documented case demonstrated CSFP associated with nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and prolonged repolarisation. A patient with CSFP presented with anginal chest pain and recurrent syncope and was noted to have multiple episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia on Holter monitoring and increased QTc dispersion.

## Pathophysiology

The dominant hypothesis centres on microvascular and endothelial dysfunction. CSFP is thought to reflect endothelial dysfunction, with factors such as inflammation, atherosclerosis, hematological disorders, and structural components also contributing, although its exact cause is not fully understood. Histopathological evidence supports a structural small-vessel component. Right ventricular endomyocardial biopsy in patients with angina and patent large arteries revealed pathologic small coronary arteries with fibromuscular hyperplasia, hypertrophy of the media, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial degeneration, with capillaries showing swollen endothelial cells encroaching on the lumen. Mangieri and colleagues reported analogous findings of small-vessel thickening and luminal narrowing in CSFP specifically [7]. Impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation has been demonstrated directly. Slow coronary flow in a normal coronary angiogram is a well-recognized clinical entity, but its etiopathogenesis remains unclear. Markers of endothelial injury, including reduced nitric oxide and elevated asymmetric dimethylarginine and homocysteine, have been repeatedly implicated [5,8]. Functionally, the disorder reflects increased resting microvascular resistance; invasive comparisons confirm that CSFP patients exhibit lower flow velocity and higher resting microvascular resistance than controls [9].

## Management

No therapy is formally established, and care is largely empirical. There is no standard and accepted treatment, and standard treatments for stable angina pectoris are often used to control CSFP and reduce symptoms. Agents that target the resistance microvessels appear most useful. In a controlled study, mibefradil reduced the number of vessels exhibiting TIMI-2 flow from 18 to 5 and significantly improved the TIMI frame count in those vessels, without changing epicardial vessel diameter or rate-pressure product. Intracoronary calcium-channel blockers acutely reverse the angiographic abnormality [10], and dipyridamole has shown benefit [11]. Nebivolol, which augments nitric oxide signalling, improves endothelial function and symptoms: nebivolol is effective at improving endothelial function in patients with slow coronary flow, controls chest pain, decreases CRP, and has favorable effects on brachial artery dilation. Statins, dipyridamole and endothelin-A receptor blockade (zibotentan) have all been explored, reflecting the inflammatory and endothelin-related dimensions of the disorder [12].

## Conclusion

CSFP is a clinically meaningful microvascular coronary disorder, not merely an angiographic curiosity. Since its clinical relevance is now being appreciated, further research is recommended to better elucidate the pathology of this phenomenon. Standardised diagnostic criteria, reliable correlation with invasive microvascular indices, and adequately powered therapeutic trials remain priorities.
